title: Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems
description: Charlotte Smith's first book and the volume that made her name: a collection of sonnets and shorter lyrics from the pen of a wife and mother turned professional writer. The poems give voice to a woman dispossessed of home and expectation, addressing the seaside, the night, melancholy, lost hope, and the ruins of her family's property claims. Reissued throughout the 1780s and 1790s in enlarged editions that added new sonnets, it established the sonnet as a vehicle of female distress and made Smith the most imitated poetic voice of her decade.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers self-contained lyric meditations rather than a narrative. Sonnets complain of fortune, of a love fixed on an unattainable or departed object, of exile from home and from a paternal inheritance, and of the consolation offered by landscape, solitude, and the contemplation of death; poems addressed to the sea, to the moon, to melancholy, and to deceased friends carry the argument that sensibility and poverty are the true education of the poet. Later issues added new sonnets and prose matter, enlarging the same repertory of complaint and consolation.
narrative_structure: A collection, not a sequence with a plot: numbered sonnets and lyrics follow one another in an arrangement that stresses variety of mood rather than progression, so that the reader assembles a persona from repeated situations of mourning, seaside reverie, and disappointed hope.
principal_characters: the poet-speaker of the sonnets; an idealised absent beloved; departed friends and relations remembered in the elegies; personified Melancholy, Hope, and Fortune
literary_form: Romantic Sonnet Revival; Sonnet Sequence; Elegy
meter_and_prosody: Fourteen-line sonnets and shorter lyrics in iambic pentameter, with Smith's characteristic blend of Italian-style octave-and-sestet patterns and English closing couplets, and frequent exclamatory, apostrophic address; the diction is deliberately plaintive and musical, in the manner later reviewers credited her with helping to refashion for the 1780s and 1790s.
historical_context: Published while Smith was legally dependent on her husband Benjamin Smith and fighting the generations-long Chancery suit over the inheritance she had brought into the marriage; her imprisonment-adjacent poverty and the King's Bench confinement of her husband in late 1783 belong to the same decade of crisis that the book's rhetoric of sorrow converts into publication. The sonnet, then a scarce and somewhat antiquated form, was being revived by a group of writers, and Smith's volume, repeatedly enlarged and reissued, became its best-known vehicle.
literary_significance: Elegiac Sonnets is the founding book of the 1780s-1790s vogue for the sensibility sonnet and one of the most influential volumes of the preromantic and Romantic period; its identification of the sonnet with a feminine voice of bereavement and financial dependence shaped the form's revival by Smith's contemporaries and successors, including the writers of the Lyrical Ballads generation, and it created the public persona on which all her later fiction and poetry depended.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; no serious dispute attaches to the volume, though the number and ordering of poems change between issues, so citations should specify the edition used.
bibliographical_notes: First issue London 1784, imprint J. Dodsley (ESTC T32495); a third edition was printed in 1786 (ESTC T32497) and further enlarged editions followed, including issues of 1789, 1792, 1795, 1797, 1800, all recorded under the title Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems; modern scholarly editions reprint the volume from the 1784 text.

title: Celestina
description: Charlotte Smith's third published novel, following Emmeline and Ethelinde, and the first of the fictions she wrote after her husband's imprisonment and her life apart from him had made her the family's breadwinner; it appeared in four volumes in 1791. It follows a young woman raised and disposed of by guardians who are not her parents, and traces the discovery of her true birth, her education in sensibility and principle, and her marriage, against a social analysis of inherited property, paternal authority, and the limited options of women. Its Alpine scenery and its portrait of an aristocratic French household on the eve of 1789 give the domestic plot a political breadth unusual in fiction of the moment.
plot_or_argument: Celestina, a young woman brought up in a household not her own and made the object of other people's financial and social calculations, is kept from knowing her parents and from choosing her own marriage; the novel recounts her long separation from the man she loves, the exposure of the interests that govern her fortune, and the eventual recovery of a lawful birth and of the marriage her inclinations had always marked out. The action is continuously interrupted by argument on the injustice of disposing of wards and heiresses in marriage, on the abuse of guardianship and of paternal authority, and on the idleness and corruption of great wealth, with set-piece passages among the Alps and in France before and after 1789.
narrative_structure: A four-volume novel of formation in the third person, organized around the slow revelation of the heroine's parentage, with embedded letters and tale-within-tale passages, and a double setting that carries the plot from England and the Savoyard and Alpine country to France on the eve of the Revolution.
principal_characters: Celestina; the heroine's guardian and the interests that control her fortune; the man she loves and is long denied; the French aristocratic household of the Alpine and Parisian episodes
literary_form: Sentimental and Domestic Novel; Novel of Manners and Fashion; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
meter_and_prosody: Prose romance in regular paragraphing; no metrical design is present, though the narrative's address to the reader and its set-piece descriptions of mountain scenery are shaped by the cadences of Smith's own sonnet prose.
historical_context: Written and published in the years of Smith's separation from Benjamin Smith and of her increasing reliance on the press, and in the immediate aftermath of 1789, when French aristocratic society was being reinterpreted in Britain as a system of abuse. Its treatment of guardianship and of the disposition of an heiress draws on the family litigations and Chancery dependency that had consumed Smith's adulthood.
literary_significance: Celestina established Smith as a novelist of property and feeling whose domestic plots conduct explicit argument about coverture, guardianship, and the marriage market; it opened the sequence of her fictions that later criticism reads as a sustained analysis of women's economic dependence, and its Alpine and pre-revolutionary French settings anticipated the political geography of her later novels.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name on the title page; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1791 in four volumes, imprint T. Cadell (ESTC T73501); modern scholarly reprints follow the first edition.

title: Desmond
description: Charlotte Smith's fourth published novel and the most openly radical of her fictions, written in letters and published at the height of the British controversy over the French Revolution. A young man of principle, Lionel Desmond, narrates his own education, his friendship with the political exile Verney, his unfortunate first marriage, arranged by interest, and his love for Geraldine Verney, while the book argues in favour of popular liberty, against hereditary government, and for the right of a wife to escape a marriage without affection. Its enthusiasm for the French cause made it a byword for Jacobin fiction in the 1790s.
plot_or_argument: Desmond's letters describe a country upbringing, an early and uncongenial marriage arranged by interest, the protection of the political exile Verney and his daughter Geraldine, and the long legal and familial obstruction that keeps the woman he loves out of his reach; interleaved with the story are debates on the French Revolution, the rights of men, standing armies, and the condition of women in marriage, so that the resolution of the private plot is made to depend on the same principles that the public argument defends.
narrative_structure: A largely epistolary novel: the correspondence of Desmond, of Geraldine Verney, and of the exiled Verney carries both plot and argument, and the exchange of letters is used to place competing readings of the French Revolution inside one fictional society.
principal_characters: Lionel Desmond; Geraldine Verney; Mr. Bethel, Desmond's friend; Verney, the political exile and father of Geraldine; the family interests that arrange Desmond's first marriage
literary_form: Epistolary Fiction; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel
meter_and_prosody: Prose correspondence in letters of varying length; the style moves between colloquial argument and declamatory political rhetoric, and verse quotations are interspersed as sententious comment.
historical_context: Published in 1792, the year of the greatest vogue and alarm for revolutionary argument in England, in the circle of writing shaped by Godwin's political philosophy and by the dispute between Wollstonecraft's defenders and her attackers; Smith's own dependence on the proceeds of the book, and her separation from her husband, made its plea for the release of wives and for professional independence a personal as well as a political statement.
literary_significance: Desmond is one of the boldest English novels of the 1790s to take the French Revolution side-by-side with the marriage question, and it is central to the recovered history of radical women's writing; its insistence that the oppression of women and of subjects are one argument made it a key text for the study of philosophical fiction, and its epistolary method showed how doctrinaire debate could be fictionalized without allegory.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed. Earlier scholarship confused its publication year, and the 1792 date is now settled by the contemporary imprint and reviews.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1792 as Desmond. A novel, in three volumes, by G. G. J. and J. Robinson, Pater-noster-Row (ESTC T73500); modern scholarly editions reprint the 1792 text.

title: The Emigrants, A Poem, in Two Books
description: Charlotte Smith's most ambitious poem and the first long blank-verse meditation by a woman poet on the French Revolution as an English coastal spectacle: French refugees, driven out by war and proscription, are watched on the Sussex cliffs and the Downs, and their dispossession becomes the occasion for a national poem about exile, charity, and the failure of revolutionary hope. Written in two books dated November 1792 and April 1793 and offered in the lineage of Cowper's The Task, it converts topographical description into political and moral argument.
plot_or_argument: Book I, set on the Sussex cliffs in November 1792, follows the coming of the émigrés, the suffering of the dispossessed French families, and the poet's own recollection of exile, and turns the landscape of the beach and the channel into a commentary on the Revolution and on the war now beginning between Britain and France. Book II, dated April 1793 and set on the Downs, widens the meditation to the causes and consequences of war, to the fate of the poor at home as well as of the refugees abroad, and to the disappointed expectation of liberty, closing in a mood of resigned charity rather than of prophecy.
narrative_structure: A poem in two books, each anchored in a dated season and a named stretch of coast and downland; the movement is that of Cowperian conversation poetry, where walking and looking generate reflection, and where the émigrés and the local poor supply the human cases on which the argument turns.
principal_characters: the poet-walker of the Sussex shore; the French émigré families; the labouring and fishing poor of the English coast; the distant actors of the Revolution and of the declared war
literary_form: Nature Lyric and Meditation; Meditative Blank Verse; Topographical and Descriptive Poetry
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of self-contained lines and passages, with the suspended syntax, apostrophe, and descriptive enumeration characteristic of blank verse after Cowper and Thomson; the poem's rhetorical cadences carry its political argument.
historical_context: Published in the spring of 1793, the month Britain declared war on revolutionary France, when the arrival of émigrés made the Revolution a visible social problem on the south coast, and when Smith, who had spent part of her childhood in France, wrote from her own experience of dispossession and dependence. Its address to Cowper locates it in a tradition of national poetry that was being rapidly politicised by the Revolution controversy.
literary_significance: The Emigrants is a central work of women's political poetry in the 1790s and an important early instance of Romantic coastal topography used to think about revolution, refugee hospitality, and war; it shows the conversation-poem and blank-verse meditation traditions being reshaped by a female professional writer, and it is now read as a necessary precedent for the Lyrical Ballads politics of poverty and landscape.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1793 as The emigrants, a poem, in two books. By Charlotte Smith, printed for T. Cadell, the Strand, quarto, ix, [3], 68 (i.e. 60) pages (ESTC T32633); reprinted in the collected poems and in modern scholarly editions.

title: The Old Manor House
description: Charlotte Smith's most elaborate novel and, by general consent, the greatest of her fictions: the story of Orlando Somerive, disinherited by an eccentric will, and of his love for Monimia, a dependent of the family whose known servitude makes any marriage between them a social scandal. Set between an English manor house, the American war, and the law, the book conducts a sustained analysis of property, entail, primogeniture, depopulation, and the treatment of the poor, and it is now standardly read as a Jacobin novel in the full sense.
plot_or_argument: Orlando, the younger son of the family that ought to be his, is cut off from the estate by his grandfather's will and by his father's compliance; he serves as a volunteer in America, returns to find Monimia, the gentlewoman's dependent he loves, exposed to the designs of other men, and struggles through legal stratagem and social penalty to establish both his right and his marriage. Around that plot the novel gathers portraits of an attorney, a disinherited heir, a decayed manor, and a village emptied by enclosure and by the changes of agricultural property.
narrative_structure: A multi-volume novel in the third person with a picaresque American-war episode and a legal-plot mechanism, alternating between country-house satire, sentimental courtship, and political narration; the two halves of Orlando's experience at home and abroad are held together by the sustained argument about inheritance.
principal_characters: Orlando Somerive; Monimia Morysine; the Somerive family and its attorney and dependants; the American war officers and prisoners of Orlando's episode
literary_form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel; Novel of Manners and Fashion
meter_and_prosody: Prose romance; Smith's narration is interrupted by embedded verse quotations and by set descriptive passages in the rhythms of her topographical poetry.
historical_context: Published in the same year as The Emigrants and immediately after Desmond, when Smith was supporting herself and her children entirely by the press and was deep in the Chancery litigation that had already absorbed a generation of her family's inheritance; its treatment of disputed succession, of the law's delay, and of a countryside emptied by enclosure and depopulation is drawn from the disputes over estate property and tenancy that her own suit dramatized.
literary_significance: The Old Manor House is the novel that secured Smith's standing in the history of English fiction, and is valued as the most complete fusion in her work of sentimental plot and economic argument; its treatment of inheritance, service, and class-crossed desire makes it a key text for the study of 1790s radical fiction and for the prehistory of the condition-of-property novel.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1793, in four volumes, for John Bell, Duke Street, Lincoln's Inn Fields (ESTC T71314); modern scholarly editions reprint the first edition.

title: The Banished Man
description: Charlotte Smith's novel of political exile published between The Old Manor House and her books for young readers, a narrative that interweaves several plots and several countries around characters driven from home by the French Revolution and by aristocratic tyranny. Its subject, announced in its title, is banishment as a condition: the loss of country, property, and protection, and the attempt of generous minds to sustain principle in exile. The book also contains a Gothic romance strand that makes it one of Smith's clearest engagements with the literature of terror.
plot_or_argument: Characters displaced from France and from other European countries pursue, across separate plots, the same conditions of proscription, dependence, and threatened inheritance; a tale of confined and pursued heroine is embedded in the larger narrative of exile, and the novel's resolution depends on the exposure of the interest and tyranny that produced the banishment, rather than on any single hero's education.
narrative_structure: An interlaced multi-plot novel of exile, combining political narrative with an inset Gothic romance; the separate stories are bound together by their shared situation of proscription and dependency rather than by a single point of view.
principal_characters: the banished families and their European hosts; the pursued heroine of the inset Gothic story; the interested kinsmen and patrons who procure the exiles' disinheritance
literary_form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Historical Novel and Romance
meter_and_prosody: Prose romance; the Gothic inset passages are written in the heightened descriptive register of the romance of terror, with verse quotations used as moral comment.
historical_context: Written and published in the darkest year of the British debate about the Revolution, when émigré settlement in England was a daily spectacle and when government repression had silenced many of Smith's radical acquaintances; her own dependence on copyright and subscription, and the failure of her hopes of a French restoration, inform the book's treatment of exile and of charity.
literary_significance: The Banished Man is important as the most sustained novel of the 1790s to make political exile its governing condition and to combine it with Gothic machinery, and it is now cited in discussions of women's revolutionary fiction and of the migration of Gothic plot into questions of proscription and refuge.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1794 for T. Cadell Junior, the Strand (ESTC T70700); reprinted in modern scholarly editions of Smith's fiction.

title: Rural Walks: In Dialogues
description: Charlotte Smith's first book for young readers and the first part of a trilogy of educational dialogues continued by Rambles Farther (1796) and Minor Morals (1798). A set of prose dialogues put among walks and conversations in the country, it teaches a girl and her relations to read the landscape, the weather, plants, animals, and social conduct by inquiry rather than by lesson, and it converts the country walk into a method of instruction. Its argumentative, anti-sentimental handling of the child's questions makes it a distinctive contribution to 1790s educational writing.
plot_or_argument: Members of a family and a young female relation talk their way through a series of country excursions, drawing moral, historical, natural-historical, and social instruction from what they see; the dialogues correct vanity, prejudice, and false sensibility, and insist on the education of judgement, on the dignity of labour, and on the duties of the rich towards their poor neighbours.
narrative_structure: Twelve prose dialogues, each a self-contained walk or conversation with a topic of its own, without continuous plot; instruction is delivered by question and correction rather than by narrative.
principal_characters: the Woodfield family of the dialogues; their young female relation who asks and is corrected; the elder interlocutors who guide the conversation
literary_form: Juvenile, School and Educational Book; Conduct, Education, and Domestic Prose
meter_and_prosody: Plain prose dialogue in short conversational turns, with occasional quotations of verse as sententious point; no metrical design proper.
historical_context: Written for the expanding market in books for young women at the moment when Smith was supporting her children entirely by her pen, and in the intellectual climate of the 1790s educational dialogue, in which natural history, politics, and moral reasoning were taught conversationally rather than by catechism.
literary_significance: Rural Walks is valued as a serious piece of Romantic-era educational theory in fictional form, and as a feminine antipastoral that refuses to sentimentalize the countryside; it is a standard example in the history of children's literature of the didactic dialogue turned to political and economic instruction.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1795, in two volumes, for T. Cadell Junior, the Strand (ESTC T98085), with the title Rural Walks, in dialogues; collected with Rambles Farther and Minor Morals in the modern multi-volume edition of Smith's works.

title: Marchmont
description: Charlotte Smith's novel of the law and of Gothic injustice, published in four volumes in the same year as her wreck narrative and her collected poems. Althea Dacres, a young woman of fortune and principle, finds herself the prey of legal contrivance and of the interests of those set over her, while the character Marchmont, bound to her by an early attachment, pursues his own ruinous career. The book turns the machinery of conveyancing, custody, and suit into an exposure of a society in which property can be stolen by procedure, and it uses castle and mountain scenery to give that exposure a Gothic emphasis.
plot_or_argument: The novel follows Althea Dacres through the attempts of guardians, lawyers, and kinsmen to intercept her fortune and control her marriage, and follows Marchmont, whose passionate nature and misplaced loyalty destroy his prospects, until the fraud practised on the heroine is unmasked and her birth and rights established; the two histories meet in a resolution that is made possible only by the failure of the legal schemes that had seemed invincible.
narrative_structure: A four-volume third-person narrative with two converging careers, a heroine's story of custody and contrivance and a young man's story of self-destructive attachment; legal explanation and Gothic scenery alternate with sentimental analysis.
principal_characters: Althea Dacres; Marchmont; the lawyers, guardians, and interested kinsmen who scheme against the heroine's fortune
literary_form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Sentimental and Domestic Novel
meter_and_prosody: Prose romance; the scenery passages of the Gothic episodes are written in a descriptive manner continuous with Smith's topographical verse, and verse quotations point the moral of the action.
historical_context: Written while Smith's own family cause in Chancery, the suit over the inheritance she had brought into her marriage, had been pending in the Court of Chancery since the 1770s and had consumed the income it was meant to secure; the novel's treatment of law as an instrument of depredation, and of a woman's inability to command her own property, transcribes her professional and personal experience of litigation into fiction.
literary_significance: Marchmont is Smith's sharpest indictment of the law of property and of the exposure of women to guardianship and procedure, and it is valued for the way it fuses Gothic romance with economic and legal realism; it is now read as an important document of the 1790s critique of inheritance, and as a link between the Gothic of the 1790s and the later fiction of legal dispossession.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1796, in four volumes, for Sampson Low, Pater-noster-Row (ESTC T70720); reprinted in modern scholarly editions of Smith's fiction.

title: A Narrative of the Loss of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont Transports
alternative_titles: Narrative of the Loss of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont Transports
description: A short prose narrative by Charlotte Smith recording the loss of the transport vessels Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont, drawn up, as its title page states, from information taken on the spot, and published to raise money for a survivor of the wrecks and her infant child. It is a work of emergency charity writing in which accurate maritime detail, distress, and the appeal to the reader's benevolence are combined, and it shows Smith turning her name and her style to immediate practical use.
plot_or_argument: The narrative reconstructs the departure, the storm, the loss of the three transports, and the sufferings and escapes of those on board, naming the circumstances of the wreck and of survival with the particularity of report rather than of romance; the account closes with the case of the surviving woman and her child, for whose benefit the whole profit of the pamphlet was assigned.
narrative_structure: A single continuous prose narrative without chapters of art, moving from the voyage to the disaster and then to the condition of the survivors, with the appeal for subscriptions framed as the occasion of publication.
principal_characters: the passengers and crews of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont; the unfortunate survivor and her infant child for whom the book was published
literary_form: Prose; Polemic, Pamphlet, and Open Letter
meter_and_prosody: Plain prose of report and address, in the syntax of the printed letter or pamphlet appeal; no metrical design.
historical_context: Published in a year of heavy maritime loss along the English coast and of convoy disaster, and at a moment when Smith's own earnings were irregular and her family dependant on her; the volume belongs to the philanthropic pamphlet literature of the 1790s, in which a known author's name was used to convert distress into subscription.
literary_significance: The narrative matters as a document of Smith's professional method and of the maritime and charitable writing of the 1790s: it shows the same writer who made wreck and exile the matter of verse and fiction turning the real disaster of the transports into a factual appeal, and it is cited in the history of women's philanthropic publication.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; the work is occasionally listed among Smith's minor prose rather than among her fiction, but its attribution to her is not disputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1796 for Sampson Low and C. Law, Weymouth (ESTC T98238), the profit declared on the title page to be for the benefit of a survivor of the wrecks and her infant child; collected with Smith's juvenile and minor prose in the modern multi-volume edition of her works.

title: The Young Philosopher
description: Charlotte Smith's last novel and the darkest of her political fictions: the story of a generous young man of principle whose idealism is destroyed by the failure of the French Revolution and by the condition of England in the 1790s, and who finally quits Europe for America. Written during her London stays of 1797 and 1798 and published in the summer of 1798, after the collapse of revolutionary expectation and during the war and repression that followed, it converts the history of a decade into the education and undoing of a single mind.
plot_or_argument: The young philosopher is formed by reading, by friendship, and by enthusiasm for liberty; he encounters in England a world of interest, dependence, and enforced idleness, loses the woman he loves to considerations of fortune, and sees the cause he espoused degenerate into tyranny and war; the novel ends with his resolution to seek in America the independence that England refused him, while the women and dependants he leaves behind are provided for by the kindness of those the plot had earlier condemned as vulgar.
narrative_structure: A multi-volume novel of the education and failure of an enthusiast, told in the third person with letters and papers interspersed, and organized as a series of disillusionments: philosophical, amatory, political, and finally national, resolved by emigration.
principal_characters: the young philosopher of the title; the woman he loves and cannot marry; his patron and his rival; the family and dependants left behind
literary_form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel; Novel of Manners and Fashion
meter_and_prosody: Prose narrative containing embedded verse and letter papers; the philosophical argument is delivered in formal set-piece speech as well as in dialogue.
historical_context: Conceived and written during Smith's stays in London in the summers of 1797 and 1798, and published in the summer of 1798, when the failure of the French Revolution, the repression that followed the war, and the collapse of radical expectation had made enthusiasm for liberty untenable in England; the suit in Chancery over the inheritance that had engaged her family since the 1770s was still undetermined, and her own sense of a closed future informs the novel's argument that principle cannot be lived under existing English conditions.
literary_significance: The Young Philosopher is read as the most explicit record in fiction of the extinction of revolutionary hope in England, and it is a key text for the history of radical sentiment and of the idea of America as a refuge; its ending, which abandons Europe rather than reforming it, marks a decisive stage in the political imagination of the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1798 for T. Cadell, the Strand (ESTC T71900), in the standard multi-volume form; reprinted in modern scholarly editions of Smith's works.

title: Conversations, Introducing Poetry to the Young
description: Charlotte Smith's last educational work, issued in two volumes by Joseph Johnson in 1804, in which an elder sister and brother teach their younger relations to read and value poetry by conversation on walks and at home. The volume was also a repository of Smith's own shorter verse: several of the poems introduced and quoted there reappeared after her death in Beachy Head, and the book therefore preserves the last stage of her poetic as well as her pedagogical practice.
plot_or_argument: The dialogues put poems and passages of poetry into the mouths and hands of children and of their instructress, using commentary, correction, and recollection to teach taste, sympathy, and moral judgement; the conversations argue that poetry is a form of knowledge proper to youth, and they model an education founded on pleasure and inquiry rather than on rote.
narrative_structure: Conversational and dialogic prose framed as family instruction, with quoted verse and explanatory comment, continuing the method of Rural Walks and Rambles Farther but turning specifically to the teaching of poetry.
principal_characters: the young pupils of the conversations; their elder sisters and brothers who conduct the teaching; the poets quoted and explained
literary_form: Juvenile, School and Educational Book; Conduct, Education, and Domestic Prose
meter_and_prosody: Prose dialogue interspersed with quoted lyric and descriptive verse in the traditional metres of the poems selected, some of them Smith's own.
historical_context: Published in the last years of Smith's life, when her income depended on commissioned and educational work and when her juvenile trilogy had established her authority in children's publishing; it belongs to the same Joseph Johnson circle that had printed her poetry and fiction for two decades, and its poems were reserved for the posthumous volume that appeared in 1807.
literary_significance: Conversations is important as Smith's statement of a poetics for the young and as the source of her late shorter lyrics; it documents the transmission of Romantic verse into the educational market, and it preserves the last poems she lived to see prepared for the press.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1804, in two volumes, for Joseph Johnson, St Paul's Church-Yard; poems introduced here were republished posthumously in Beachy Head, and Other Poems (1807), and the work is collected with Smith's juvenile writing in the modern multi-volume edition of her works.

title: Beachy Head, and Other Poems
description: Charlotte Smith's last and greatest volume of verse, published after her death at her own expense from copies she had prepared: the long topographical-descriptive poem Beachy Head, together with sonnets and shorter lyrics. From the cliff of the Sussex headland the poem takes in geology, natural history, the fishing and wrecking of the coast, the fate of the poor, and the poet's own age, dependence, and approaching death, in a blank verse of unusual range that opens with one of the great cosmological panoramas of Romantic poetry.
plot_or_argument: The title poem rises from the view from Beachy Head to the turning earth and the remoter planets, returns to the chalk cliff, its ruined chapel and its tradition of hermits and outcasts, and passes through the fishing, wrecking, and poverty of the Sussex coast to a meditation on the poet's own exhaustion, bereavement, and death; the accompanying sonnets and shorter lyrics repeat the same repertoire of melancholy, natural observation, and consolation, several of them written and published earlier in her life.
narrative_structure: A volume dominated by one long descriptive-meditative poem in the manner of Thomson and Cowper, whose movement is associational and from which the shorter poems and sonnets form a second, lyric division.
principal_characters: the poet on the headland; the hermit and the outcast of the cliff tradition; the fishermen, wreckers, and poor of the Sussex coast; the mourner of the shorter poems
literary_form: Topographical and Descriptive Poetry; Nature Lyric and Meditation; Romantic Sonnet Revival
meter_and_prosody: Beachy Head is written in decasyllabic blank verse of long, suspended periods, with elaborate descriptive enumeration and apostrophe; the remainder of the volume supplies Petrarchan and hybrid sonnets and shorter lyrics in varied stanzaic and metrical patterns.
historical_context: Prepared during Smith's last years of increasing illness, poverty, and anxiety for her children, and issued in 1807, a year after her death, printed for the author and sold by her long-time publisher; its coastal setting is the country of her own residences, and its treatment of geological deep time, natural history, and the suffering of the poor responds to the scientific and topographical writing of the 1790s and 1800s.
literary_significance: Beachy Head is now recognized as one of the major long poems of the Romantic period and as the most powerful statement of a women's topographical and scientific imagination between the Revolution and its disappointment; its combination of the sublime, natural history, and the politics of poverty has made it central to the recovery of Smith and to the redefinition of Romantic landscape poetry.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name from manuscripts she prepared; attribution is undisputed, though the volume was posthumous and its final arrangement was made by others.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1807, printed for the author and sold by J. Johnson, as Beachy Head, and Other Poems; the poems introduced in Conversations, Introducing Poetry to the Young reappear here, and the volume is reprinted from the 1807 text in the modern collected poems.

title: Poems. By Mrs. M. Robinson. In Two Volumes
description: Mary Robinson's first collected volume of verse, the book by which she converted the notoriety of the Perdita episode into a literary career. Gathering her lyric and occasional poetry, some of it already circulated in the periodical press, it presents an accomplished occasional and elegiac poet - addresses to the moment, meditations on loss, and sonnet-like numbers drawn from her own history - and consolidates the persona of the English Sappho she had been building since her Della Cruscan prominence. Its second volume appeared two years later with different publishers, evidence of the unstable bookselling arrangements under which she worked.
plot_or_argument: The volume is a collection rather than an argument: its poems mourn lost children and lost love, describe retirement, autumn, and the seaside, complain of the cruelty of fame and of the price of a woman's reputation, and offer sententious reflection on mutability and endurance; several numbers turn on the disparity between the public notoriety of the narrator and the private sufferings she records.
narrative_structure: Two volumes of separate lyrics and short descriptive poems, arranged without sustained sequence, the two volumes appearing years apart; the reader assembles an autobiographical persona from repeated situations of mourning, exposure, and complaint.
principal_characters: the poet-speaker of the volumes; the lost beloved and the dead children of the elegies; Fame and Misfortune as apostrophised powers
literary_form: Lyric; Romantic Sonnet Revival; Elegy
meter_and_prosody: Conventionally regular decasyllabic and octosyllabic lines in lyric stanzas and in sonnet forms, with a musical, complaint-driven diction inherited from the Della Cruscan and sentimental traditions and frequent apostrophe.
historical_context: Published after Robinson's separation from Thomas Robinson, her ruin in the public eye following the rupture with the Prince of Wales in the early 1780s, and her years on the Continent, and at the moment when her association with Robert Merry and the Della Cruscan vogue was making her the most talked-about female poet in London; like Charlotte Smith she turned legal and financial dependence into a publishing career, and her first volume was a deliberate opening of that campaign.
literary_significance: The volume established Robinson as a professional poet of the 1790s and is the basis of her reputation as one of the principal agents of the sonnet revival and of the lyrical vogue that preceded the Lyrical Ballads; it documents the making of a public female poetic identity out of scandal, and it is now read as an essential part of the popular Romanticism that Wordsworthian scholarship long effaced.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name as Mrs. M. Robinson; attribution is undisputed, though the two volumes were issued separately and bibliographical statements that treat the collection as a single 1791 event are inaccurate.
bibliographical_notes: Volume the first published London 1791 for John Bell; volume the second followed in 1793 from J. Evans and T. Becket, as recorded in the Jackson Bibliography of Romantic Poetry; the whole is reprinted in the modern collected edition of Robinson's works.

title: Vancenza; or, The Dangers of Credulity
description: Mary Robinson's first novel, a two-volume gothic romance written in letters and published by subscription the year after her first volume of poetry. Its heroine, Vancenza, is a girl formed by the extravagant reading of romance and of the marvellous, and the plot subjects her credulity to real persecution, so that the book at once exploits and criticizes the machinery of the novel of terror. Its large subscription list shows how quickly Robinson translated poetical fame into novel-reading capital.
plot_or_argument: Vancenza, an imaginative young woman brought up on tales of the marvellous and persuaded of preternatural intimations, is drawn into a succession of real dangers engineered by interested and tyrannical men; the narrative of her trials, told in letters, converts the expectations formed by romance into evidence of the vulnerability of women left uninstructed, and resolves her sufferings by the exposure of the fraud and violence that produced them.
narrative_structure: An epistolary gothic novel in two volumes, the story delivered in letters from the heroine and her companions, with romance-style suspense and explanation used in the service of an argument about reading and belief.
principal_characters: Vancenza; the tyrannical and interested men who persecute her; the female companions and protectors to whom she writes
literary_form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Epistolary Fiction
meter_and_prosody: Prose correspondence; the novel's heightened situations are phrased in the diction of Robinson's descriptive and elegiac verse, and verse is quoted as sententious comment on the action.
historical_context: Published in the same years as the most productive phase of the English gothic, and immediately after Robinson had begun her public career as a poet and performer dependent on subscriptions and on her own credit; its title-page promise of a moral against credulity belongs to the 1790s debate about the dangers of novel-reading, in which women's fiction was simultaneously a commercial and an educational risk.
literary_significance: Vancenza is an early and instructive instance of a woman writer using gothic machinery to argue against the credulity that gothic feeds, and it marks the start of Robinson's remarkable sequence of eight novels, of which Walsingham and The Natural Daughter are the most considered; its subscription success is a fact of the first importance for the economic history of women's writing in the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1792, in two volumes, a subscription issue with a list of about six hundred subscribers recorded in the first edition; reprinted in the modern scholarly edition of Robinson's fiction.

title: Monody to the Memory of the Late Queen of France
description: Mary Robinson's public lament for Marie Antoinette, issued as a separate poem within months of the execution of the French queen and one of the most conspicuous political lyrics of 1793. Casting the death as the matter of a formal monody, it transforms an executed queen into the emblem of civilized suffering under revolutionary terror, and it declared Robinson's royalist and humane politics at a moment when the British debate about France was being closed by war and repression.
plot_or_argument: The poet mourns the fate of the queen of France, traces her fall from splendour to the tribunal and the scaffold, sets domestic and conjugal virtue against public violence, and answers the spectacle of the Revolution with indignation at its proceedings and with consolation drawn from the endurance of those who mourn; the poem makes the private grief of the lament the ground of a public political judgment.
narrative_structure: A single continuous monody in the convention of the formal lament, moving from apostrophe through historical recapitulation and denunciation to consolation, without division into books.
principal_characters: the mourning poet; Marie Antoinette, the late queen of France; the actors and spectators of the revolutionary trial and execution
literary_form: Elegy; Political and Revolutionary Verse; Lyric
meter_and_prosody: A monody in the manner of the formal lament: sustained decasyllabic meditative verse in the elevated diction of the occasional elegy, with apostrophe and exclamatio governing the movement of the lines.
historical_context: Published in the year of the execution of Louis XVI and of the British declaration of war on France, when sympathy for the queen was a politically charged act and when Robinson, like her contemporaries, was writing revolution controversy for immediate sale; the poem was admired by contemporaries and quickly became one of her most reprinted occasional pieces.
literary_significance: The Monody is a document of the sudden English royalist elegy of 1793 and of the part women poets took in the revolution debate, and it is often cited as evidence that Robinson's politics cannot be assimilated to the radicalism of her friends; the poem's use of landscape mourning for a political end is characteristic of the decade's verse.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1793 for J. Evans and T. Becket, as recorded in the Jackson Bibliography of Romantic Poetry; reprinted in the collected edition of Robinson's poetical works.

title: Sappho and Phaon. In a Series of Legitimate Sonnets, with Other Poems, and a Ballad
description: Mary Robinson's most important volume of verse and a central book of the 1790s sonnet revival: a series of sonnets cast as the correspondence of Sappho and Phaon, in which the ancient poetess becomes the voice of a woman pleading, loving, and complaining in the first person. With its accompanying shorter poems and a ballad, the volume claims legitimacy for the sonnet as a form of female passion and argument, and it deliberately rewrites the Petrarchan tradition from the side of the mistress rather than the lover.
plot_or_argument: The sonnets dramatize Sappho's love for Phaon, her remonstrance, her jealousy, and her abandonment, and draw the anecdote of the Grecian poetess's leap and death into the sequence; the interwoven miscellaneous poems and the ballad extend the same argument about inconstant love, female reputation, and the poet's power, so that the volume's story is the history of a woman's passion answered by coldness and finally converted into verse.
narrative_structure: A sonnet sequence with a loose narrative core - the Sappho and Phaon story - supported by a group of separate lyric and descriptive poems and a closing ballad; the progression is from address and hope through complaint and jealousy to resignation.
principal_characters: Sappho; Phaon; the rival object of Phaon's regard; the Grecian legend of the poetess's leap
literary_form: Romantic Sonnet Revival; Sonnet Sequence; Lyric
meter_and_prosody: Sonnets of fourteen iambic pentameter lines in the Italian manner, with the volume's own emphasis on legitimate and correctly-modelled sonnet structure; the accompanying lyrics and the ballad use shorter popular stanzas.
historical_context: Published in the middle of the extraordinary vogue for the sonnet that Robinson and Charlotte Smith together created, and after the Della Cruscan period of her fame; her use of Sappho as a speaking female poet is a claim of authority made at a time when her own public history as a scandalous woman still governed her reception.
literary_significance: Sappho and Phaon is one of the two or three volumes on which the 1790s revival of the English sonnet rested, and it is the most audacious instance of a woman writer appropriating the Petrarchan sequence for female desire and self-justification; it fixed Robinson's contemporary title of the English Sappho and is now indispensable to any history of the Romantic sonnet.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1796 for Hookham and Carpenter, as recorded in the Jackson Bibliography of Romantic Poetry, the title page expanding the series into legitimate sonnets with other poems and a ballad and with anecdotes of the Grecian poetess; reprinted in the collected edition of Robinson's works.

title: Walsingham; or, The Pupil of Nature. A Domestic Story
description: Mary Robinson's most ambitious novel and, by general consent, her best: a domestic story in four volumes which combines the friendship of a young writer for a generous and eccentric man with the ruin of a seduced and abandoned heroine, and which satirizes the literary, philosophical, and fashionable circles of the 1790s with a roman à clef sharpness. Its treatment of female vulnerability and its exposure of philosophical cant make it a decisive novel of the decade.
plot_or_argument: The young poet narrates his education by Walsingham, a man of principle and fortune whose benevolence is exploited by the world, and his witnessing of the trial of Isabella, a woman seduced, cast off, and driven to destitution; the two histories are interrupted by satirical portraits of the literary and philosophical society of the day, and the novel ends in the failure of virtue to be protected by law or custom.
narrative_structure: A four-volume novel with a framing first-person narrator and a plotted inset of Isabella's ruin, interlacing domestic narrative, satire of contemporary literary society, and moral argument; the tone alternates between tenderness and public accusation.
principal_characters: Walsingham; Isabella; the young poet-pupil who narrates; the profligate seducer; the satirical portraits of literary and philosophical society
literary_form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Novel of Manners and Fashion
meter_and_prosody: Prose narrative with embedded verse and letter papers; the satirical portraits are handled in a pointed, epigrammatic style continuous with her journalistic writing.
historical_context: Written in the years when Robinson's intimacy with the radical literary world, her dependence on Longman and other publishers, and her own history as a public mistress made her simultaneously an insider and an object of libel; the novel's attacks on philosophical pretence and on the sexual double standard were read by contemporaries as portraits of identifiable persons, and its finances were settled with the publisher in a payment recorded for the first edition.
literary_significance: Walsingham is the novel that shows Robinson's full command of the 1790s domestic fiction of seduction, and is valued as a satirical record of the literary field of the decade and as one of the strongest feminist analyses of seduction before the nineteenth century; its recovery has made it a standard text in the study of women's fiction of the Revolutionary era.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed, and the identification of individual satirical portraits remains a matter of scholarly argument.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1797, in four volumes, for T. N. Longman (the payment to the author being recorded in the publisher's accounts); reprinted in the modern scholarly edition of Robinson's novels.

title: A Letter to the Women of England, on the Injustice of Mental Subordination
alternative_titles: A Letter to the Women of England
description: Mary Robinson's most sustained feminist prose argument, a published letter to the women of England urging them to refuse the mental subordination that their education and their laws impose on them. Addressed to women rather than to their husbands, it complains of the denial of education, of the double standard of sexual conduct, of the confinement of wives to domestic dependence, and of the emptiness of accomplishments, and it calls on its readers to think and to write for themselves. It stands with the writing of Wollstonecraft as one of the sharp feminist statements of the 1790s.
plot_or_argument: The letter argues that women are made inferior by treatment rather than by nature: they are educated for display and not for judgement, denied the means of subsistence by the law of marriage, judged by a harsher rule than men in conduct, and encouraged to submit their minds to husbands, fathers, and opinion; Robinson answers each of these injustices with an appeal to female reason, independence, and mutual instruction, and closes by exhorting her readers to claim intellectual freedom as their birthright.
narrative_structure: A single continuous open letter in prose, developed as a sequence of grievances and refutations rather than as a narrative, with direct apostrophe to the women of England throughout.
principal_characters: the women of England as the addressed reader; husbands, fathers, and tutors as the imposed authorities; the professed advocates of female inferiority
literary_form: Polemic, Pamphlet, and Open Letter; Conduct, Education, and Domestic Prose
meter_and_prosody: Plain declamatory prose in the manner of the published letter, with balanced periods and direct address; no metrical design.
historical_context: Published in 1799, in the final years of Robinson's life, when she was ill, impoverished, and dependent on her pen, and in the decade that produced the most concentrated English debate on the condition of women; the intellectual climate of Wollstonecraft's feminism and her own experience of scandal, separation, and financial precarity give the letter's complaints about law, reputation, and dependence a directly personal ground.
literary_significance: The Letter is one of the canonical feminist polemics of the Revolutionary era and is now standard reading in the history of women's writing; its insistence that subordination is mental before it is legal, and its address to women as rational agents, make it an essential companion text to the fiction with which it is now usually anthologized.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1799 as a separate pamphlet letter addressed to the women of England; the text is preserved in facsimile in a modern anthology of writing of the Revolutionary and Romantic period and is reprinted with The Natural Daughter in a modern scholarly edition.

title: The Natural Daughter; with Portraits of the Leadenhead Family
description: Mary Robinson's last completed novel, published in two volumes in the same year as her Letter to the Women of England, and the most satirical of her fictions. Its subject is the illegitimate daughter of a man of rank, whose natural claim to consideration is set against the artificial morality of a family portrait gallery of the prosperous and the opinionated, the Leadenheads of the title. The book argues in narrative form the case for women's vulnerability that the Letter had argued in prose.
plot_or_argument: The natural daughter, acknowledged by affection but excluded by law and custom, struggles against the interest, pride, and hypocrisy of the families who protect and dispose of her; the Leadenhead portraits supply a comic exposure of genteel prejudice, mercenary marriage, and social ambition, and the heroine's trial ends only when the calculations that governed her are dismantled and her worth is acknowledged on its own terms.
narrative_structure: A two-volume novel combining a heroine's tale of exclusion with a satirical series of family portraits; the movement is between sentimental analysis and comic exposure, with letters and papers interspersed.
principal_characters: the natural daughter of the title; the Leadenhead family of the satirical portraits; the man of rank whose acknowledgment the law refuses; the marriage-market interests around the heroine
literary_form: Novel of Manners and Fashion; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel
meter_and_prosody: Prose narrative with pointed satirical description; verse and letter papers are interspersed, and the portraits are drawn in an epigrammatic manner derived from her periodical writing.
historical_context: Written in the last years of Robinson's life, when her novels were being bought by the publisher for sums recorded in his accounts and when her own public history as an acknowledged but unprotected woman made the legal position of illegitimacy and of women her natural subject; the novel's pairing in modern editions with the Letter reflects the continuity of their argument.
literary_significance: The Natural Daughter is valued as the fiction that completes Robinson's attack on the marriage market and on the legal dependence of women, and as one of the most accomplished satires of prosperous family pretension before the Regency novel; it is now read as an important stage in the development of women's social fiction in the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1799, in two volumes, for the publisher who paid a sum recorded for it in his accounts; reprinted with A Letter to the Women of England in a modern scholarly edition.

title: Lyrical Tales
description: Mary Robinson's last and most remarkable volume of poetry, a collection of narrative and lyrical tales published in 1800 and designed as a direct answer to the Lyrical Ballads of Wordsworth and Coleridge. Its ballads, metrical tales, and lyrics take as their subjects the outcast, the imprisoned, the abandoned woman, the emigrant, and the poor, in a deliberately popular stanzaic style; the volume asserts against the Lake poets an alternative theory of poetic subject, diction, and feeling, and it is now recognized as one of the central poetical books of its decade.
plot_or_argument: The poems tell short stories of distress and endurance: women betrayed and cast off, prisoners and exiles, old and destitute figures of the street and the coast, and lovers separated by fortune or death; each tale converts a situation of suffering into an appeal to sympathy, and several reflect on the poet's own exposure, dependence, and fame, so that the volume's argument is at once political, moral, and personal.
narrative_structure: A collection of separate lyrical tales and ballads, some in dialogue and some in continuous narrative, arranged so that the popular stanzaic tales and the more reflective lyrics balance one another; there is no single organizing plot.
principal_characters: the betrayed and abandoned heroines of the tales; prisoners, exiles, and emigrants; the aged and destitute figures of the street and coastal ballads; the poet's own speaker of the reflective numbers
literary_form: Lyrical Ballad and Popular Stanza; Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Lyric
meter_and_prosody: Ballad and popular stanzaic measures - octosyllabic and alternately rhymed quatrains, lyric stanzas, and simple repeated refrains - with a deliberately plain diction that imitates and answers the theory of Lyrical Ballads while keeping the music of her earlier verse.
historical_context: Published after the Lyrical Ballads of 1798 had made the tale of humble distress a school of poetry, and in the year of Robinson's final illness and death; printed for Longman and Rees by a Bristol firm and paid for at a sum recorded in the publisher's books, the volume compresses her whole career's concern with reputation, dependence, and the suffering of women into a popular form.
literary_significance: Lyrical Tales is the most complete attempt by a contemporary of Wordsworth to write an alternative book of Lyrical Ballads, and its recovery has changed the account of English verse around 1800; it shows the ballad and the metrical tale being used by a woman poet for a social argument about poverty, seduction, and exile, and it stands as one of the founding documents of popular Romanticism.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1800, printed for T. N. Longman and O. Rees, Paternoster-Row, by Biggs and Co., Bristol, as Lyrical Tales; reprinted from the first edition in the collected edition of Robinson's works and in modern anthologies of Romantic verse.

title: Memoirs of the Late Mrs. Robinson, Written by Herself
alternative_titles: Memoirs of the Late Mrs. Robinson
description: Mary Robinson's autobiographical prose, published within months of her death and written in her own hand and voice: the story of a poor Bristol childhood, a child marriage, the years on the stage, the connexion with the Prince of Wales and the name of Perdita, estrangement, and the long effort to maintain herself and her daughter by her pen. It is at once a self-defence, a history of a woman's exposure to public report, and one of the earliest English autobiographies written by a woman for publication as a means of subsistence.
plot_or_argument: The memoirs recount the author's girlhood in Bristol and her early teaching, her marriage, her years of poverty and dependence, her appearance before the public and the royal connexion that made her name notorious, the separation and the loss of reputation that followed, and her later life devoted to writing and to her daughter; the narrative conducts a continuous argument about the price paid by a woman for the protection she was given and for the independence she claimed, and it carries her story only part of the way through her own career.
narrative_structure: A first-person continuous prose autobiography, and chronological in design, with letters and personal papers interspersed; the text breaks off before the events of the author's final years and was completed for the press after her death.
principal_characters: the author as narrator of her own life; her family and early acquaintances at Bristol; the public and court figures of the Perdita years; her daughter
literary_form: Memoir and Autobiographical Prose
meter_and_prosody: Conversational prose autobiography, moving between narrative, reflection, and quoted letter; no metrical design.
historical_context: Written as Robinson's means failed and her health gave way, and published in 1801, the winter after her death at Englefield Green, in the tradition of the female apology and the professional memoir; its printing and its immediate republication in America belong to the same bookselling network that had printed her poems and novels, and its frankness about royal favour, separation, and dependence made it a scandal as well as a book.
literary_significance: The Memoirs are a foundational text for the study of Robinson, of the Perdita story, and of women's self-writing in the 1790s, and they supplied the biographical shape of her reputation for two centuries; as an autobiography that converts a notorious life into a case against the conditions of women's existence they remain one of the most quoted prose documents of Romantic-period writing.
attribution_notes: Written by Robinson herself, as the title page asserted; the closing portion and the editorial matter added after her death are by others, and quotations from the Memoirs should observe that boundary.
bibliographical_notes: First published London 1801, printed for R. Phillips, executed by C. Mercier, with contemporary republications at New York (T. and J. Swords, 1801) and Philadelphia (T. and W. Bradford, 1802); reprinted in the modern scholarly edition of Robinson's prose.
